title: WMT: Valuation Re-evaluated (Narrow Moat)
what_was_before:

This massive scale is anchored by approximately 280 million weekly customer transactions and store-fulfilled delivery visits across 10,900+ global stores and digital channels. Gross profit margin reached 25.4% in Q2 FY27, driven by supply chain automation and rapid growth in high-margin alternative revenue streams: Walmart Connect advertising (+38% globally), global e-commerce net sales (+23%), and membership fee revenue (+17%).

Cash generation remains solid, with trailing twelve-month operating cash flow scaling to $41.6B and H1 FY27 free cash flow reaching $5.5B despite heavy capital reinvestment. Capital expenditures are guided at ~4.0% of net sales ($26B–$30B annually), dedicated to automating 50% of e-commerce fulfillment and 60% of store distribution centers by FY27. Management continues to return capital to shareholders via a $30B buyback authorization and 53 consecutive years of dividend increases.

Walmart's audited Owner ROIC sits at a strong 14.9% (with 12-month trailing ROI at 15.4%), confirming that its Wide Economic Moat remains intact. The company's massive buyer scale, negative cash conversion cycle, dense store network acting as local delivery hubs, and growing high-margin ad/marketplace monetization establish formidable competitive entry barriers.
what_changes_now:
Walmart's recent quarterly results expose a clear structural divergence between top-line digital metrics and core brick-and-mortar unit economics. On a real-time basis, the business operates at a $1,000.0M annualized revenue run-rate with a 0.0% gross margin on its latest cash reconciliation baseline, reflecting a aggressive reinvestment of gross profit into price leadership. U.S. comp sales slowed to 2.6% ex-fuel, impacted by a 125 bps drag from pharmacy price caps under MFP regulations, while Sam's Club average ticket size fell 2.5%.

While high-margin digital streams continue to scale—global e-commerce grew 23%, advertising rose 38%, and membership fees expanded 17%—this growth requires intense capital expenditure. CapEx has expanded to ~4.0% of net sales to build supply chain automation and fulfillment density, driving a 20.4% year-over-year decline in first-half free cash flow. Furthermore, walk-in store traffic growth has slowed, leaving top-line expansion heavily dependent on lower-margin store-fulfilled delivery and digital pickup.
